sources.title: Mahila Suraksha booklet
sources.notes: Video-call blackmail: don't take calls from strangers, save evidence, report

sources.title: CIAD-2024-0050: Preventing online scams
sources.notes: Agencies 'will never pressure you into sending money immediately'; 'Never pay for job offers'; no UPI PIN or OTP to receive money; 'Never install remote access software on your device for anyone'

sources.title: Sanchar Saathi: Chakshu
sources.notes: Reporting suspected fraud calls, SMS and WhatsApp messages (not for money already lost; use 1930)

sources.notes: A call shown as 'International Call' cannot be from Indian authorities

sources.title: DoT advisory on calls threatening mobile disconnection
sources.notes: 'The DoT does not make calls to citizens threatening disconnection'

sources.title: UPI fraud alert
sources.notes: The UPI PIN is only for sending money

sources.title: Scam alerts
sources.notes: Read in a browser (WebFetch 403). ATO impersonation via email, SMS, calls, social media and fake sites, including 2026 variants: malware 'payment update' emails installing remote desktop software, fake appointment emails with myGov phishing, and a crypto 'non-KYC wallet' email demanding an immediate declaration call. The ATO will never threaten arrest or prosecution via email/SMS or request payment or personal details through unsolicited communication; verify on 1800 008 540.

sources.title: 2025 IC3 Annual Report
sources.date: 2026 (covers calendar 2025; release date not printed in extracted text)
sources.notes: 2025: 1,008,597 complaints, $20.877 billion losses (+26%); 60+ filed 201,266 complaints with $7.7 billion losses. Top cyber-enabled fraud by loss: investment $8.65bn, BEC $3.05bn, tech support $2.13bn, confidence/romance $929m, government impersonation $798m; crypto investment fraud $7.2bn. Crypto ATM/kiosk: 13,460 complaints, $389 million (+58%), 60+ lost $257.5m; recovery scams 10,516 complaints, $1.4 billion; gold courier scams about 725 complaints, $311.8 million.

sources.title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN-4831389 (Mrs R v HSBC UK Bank Plc, safe account scam)
sources.notes: A fake HSBC fraud-team caller (June 2023) had the victim move £9,150 to another person's account 'to keep it safe', using the reference 'god son' and the payment type 'paying friends or family'; when HSBC's genuine fraud team called, she said it was for her godson's university fees as the scammer had told her. HSBC told the ombudsman customers are sometimes coached on what story to give the bank.

sources.title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN-5540935 (Mrs W v Barclays Bank UK PLC, investment scam cash withdrawal)
sources.notes: An investment scam victim (fake 'Adams Street Partners') withdrew £7,100 cash in branch in April 2024 and gave it to a 'courier'; she told Barclays it was for 'home renovation'. The ombudsman found the scammer had given her a cover story and told her to lie about the payment purpose, and that she confirmed to a Barclays agent no one had told her to mislead the bank.

sources.title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN8143231 (Miss R v Lloyds Bank PLC, HMRC impersonation)
sources.notes: A fake HMRC caller (spoofing HMRC's real number) threatened a 63-year-old with arrest over unpaid tax, told her not to reveal the real reason because the bank would close her account, and told her to say the money was for a holiday on a prepaid travel card; she repeated this cover story to Lloyds' fraud team and branch while the scammer listened via her phone in her handbag. The ombudsman notes it is widely recognised fraudsters instruct customers to give a cover story and that banks should probe further.

sources.title: How To Avoid a Government Impersonation Scam
sources.notes: Scammers pose as SSA (number 'suspended', benefits ending), IRS (taxes owed, arrest/deportation/licence threats), Medicare, the FTC or police/courts (warrants, missed jury duty), and may tell you to move money to keep it safe or withdraw cash/buy gold to hand over. The government will never demand payment by wire, gift card, cryptocurrency or payment app, threaten arrest, or suspend your SSN; the IRS does not call about taxes without prior mailed notices.

sources.title: Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2024
sources.notes: Latest full Data Book listed on ftc.gov (no 2025 edition found at the expected URL, which returned 404). Reports 2.6 million fraud reports and over $12 billion lost in 2024; 845,806 imposter scam reports with $2.95 billion lost; bank transfers/payments had the highest aggregate losses ($2.09 billion) followed by cryptocurrency ($1.42 billion), while credit cards were most often reported; median loss for investment-related fraud $9,196.

sources.title: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.notes: Family emergency scammers pose as a relative in trouble (sometimes with an AI-cloned voice) or as a lawyer, police officer or doctor, stress urgency, and ask you to keep it secret; they ask for wire transfers, crypto, payment apps or gift card numbers. Advice: hang up, call the relative on a known number and check with others even if told to keep it secret.

sources.title: Avoiding and Reporting Gift Card Scams
sources.notes: Scammers posing as government agencies, Microsoft/Apple support, family members (sometimes voice-cloned), prize organisers, utilities, romantic interests or fake-check senders demand gift cards (Google Play, Apple, Amazon, eBay, Target); they tell victims to buy at several stores so cashiers won't get suspicious, stay on the phone, and send the number and PIN or a photo. No real business or agency will tell you to pay with a gift card.

sources.title: FTC Data Show People Reported Losing $3.5 Billion to Imposter Scams in 2025
sources.notes: Reports $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams in 2025, nearly one in three fraud reports; government impersonators about $920 million (up from $789 million in 2024) and business impersonators nearly $1 billion (up from $866 million), with bank impersonators the highest-loss business imposters; total 2025 fraud losses about $16 billion.

sources.title: Prepared Statement of the FTC on The Rising Scam Economy, Joint Economic Committee
sources.notes: Gives full-year 2025 Sentinel figures: 3 million fraud reports and $15.9 billion reported lost; over 1 million imposter reports with over $3.5 billion lost; investment scams over $7.9 billion (about half of all losses). Bank payments had the highest aggregate losses, followed by cryptocurrency; text messages were the top reported contact method and social media the top contact method by losses (over $2 billion in FY 2025).

sources.title: Refund and Recovery Scams
sources.notes: Recovery scammers buy 'sucker lists' of past victims and pose as government agencies, consumer groups or law firms, demanding upfront retainer, processing, tax or shipping fees or bank/card numbers to 'deposit' a refund. The FTC and real agencies never charge fees to help you get a refund, never ask for financial details for this, and never guarantee recovery.

sources.title: Bitcoin ATMs: A payment portal for scammers (Data Spotlight)
sources.notes: Reported Bitcoin ATM fraud losses rose nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023 and topped $65 million in 1H 2024, median loss $10,000; people 60+ were over three times as likely to report a loss and accounted for about 71% ($46 million) of losses. Most cases are government/business impersonation or tech support scams; victims are told to withdraw cash from their bank, go to a specific machine and scan a texted QR code, with the machines called 'safety lockers'.

sources.title: False alarm, real scam: how scammers are stealing older adults' life savings (Data Spotlight)
sources.notes: Reports from older adults losing $10,000+ to business/government impersonators rose from 1,790 (2020) to 8,269 (2024); $100K+ reports rose nearly sevenfold. Storylines: account misuse, information tied to a crime, or computer security problem (fake pop-ups), with hand-offs between fake bank/Amazon/Microsoft/SSA/FTC agents; victims are told to transfer money, deposit cash into Bitcoin ATMs or hand cash/gold to couriers, and kept on the phone. Payment methods for $10K+ losses: crypto 33%, bank transfer 20%, cash 16%.

sources.title: Impersonation scams: not what they used to be (Data Spotlight)
sources.notes: 2023: over 330,000 business-impersonation and nearly 160,000 government-impersonation reports, combined losses over $1.1 billion (more than 3x 2020). Describes multi-hop scams (fake Amazon to fake bank to fake FBI/FTC), fake security alerts, Geek Squad renewals with fake refund 'overpayments', bogus legal problems, and victims told to move money or load cash into Bitcoin ATMs ('safety lockers') to protect it.

sources.title: Romance scammers' favorite lies exposed (Data Spotlight)
sources.notes: 2022: nearly 70,000 romance scam reports, $1.3 billion lost, median $4,400; crypto and bank wires over 60% of losses, gift cards most frequent method (24%). Common lies: stationed at a faraway military base, offshore oil rig worker, sick/hurt/in jail, crypto investment tutor, package stuck in customs; 40% of losers were first contacted on social media, conversations moved to WhatsApp, Google Chat or Telegram.

sources.title: Paying to get paid: gamified job scams drive record losses (Data Spotlight)
sources.notes: Job scam losses topped $220 million in 1H 2024; about 20,000 task-scam reports in 1H 2024 vs about 5,000 in all of 2023; crypto losses to job scams about $41 million in 1H 2024. Task scams start with unexpected texts/WhatsApp messages, pay small early commissions for liking videos or rating products in sets of forty, then require deposits (mostly crypto) to unlock tasks or withdraw; fake group chats pressure hesitant victims.

sources.title: How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams
sources.notes: Fake pop-ups, calls, texts and search ads lead victims to fake technicians who seek remote access. A refund variant uses fake Geek Squad/McAfee/Norton renewal notices; the caller 'processes a refund', claims too much was refunded and asks the victim to send back the difference by gift card, wire/bank transfer, crypto or payment app. Real security warnings never ask you to call a number.

sources.title: Got a text about unpaid tolls? It's probably a scam
sources.notes: Texts posing as tolling agencies claim unpaid tolls with an amount and a link to a page harvesting card/bank details and personal data such as driver's licence numbers. Advice: do not click, check with the tolling agency via a known number or site, report junk or forward to 7726.

sources.title: Phishing and scams: report HMRC related phishing emails, texts and phone call scams
sources.date: First published 14 May 2025; last updated 24 November 2025
sources.notes: HMRC will never send a tax rebate notification or ask for personal or payment details by text, never offers rebates via social media, and only emails from addresses ending hmrc.gov.uk. Report texts to 60599, emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and calls via the online suspicious-call form.

sources.title: Tax scams / consumer alerts
sources.notes: Warning signs of IRS impersonators: demands for immediate payment with 'now or else' pressure, threats of arrest or deportation, no chance to question or appeal the amount, and unexpected fake tax bills.

sources.title: The seven words that reveal you're talking to a scammer: 'Move your money to a safe account'
sources.notes: Lloyds data (Jul 2025-Jun 2026): impersonation scam victims lost £3,516 on average (+10%); HMRC (+63%), broadband/mobile (+57%), solicitor (+35%), Amazon (+27%) and police/bank (+4%) impersonation rose while all impersonation fell 3%; bank and police impersonation up 18% in Q2 2026. Says criminals tell victims their own bank is involved in fraud and coach them to lie to genuine bank staff; case study of an 85-year-old told by fake police not to contact her bank, who bought £188,000 of gold collected by a fake undercover officer. Read via browser (WebFetch hit an error page).

sources.title: Continued action critical to combat fraud as annual scam losses exceed $2 billion (Targeting Scams Report 2025)
sources.notes: For calendar 2025, 481,523 combined scam reports, 274,577 with losses totalling $2.18 billion (losses up 7.8% on 2024, down 29.7% from the 2022 peak). Top five by loss: investment ($837.7m), payment re-direction ($166.8m), romance ($139.9m), phishing ($97.6m), remote access ($69.9m). People 65+ were 26.5% of Scamwatch losses; text-message scam reports fell from 77,365 to 29,058. The full report PDF (nasc.gov.au) blocked fetching.

sources.title: A-Z of cyber crime and fraud
sources.publisher: Report Fraud (City of London Police; formerly Action Fraud)
sources.notes: Old actionfraud.police.uk/a-z-of-fraud URL now redirects here (WebFetch blocked with 403; read via browser). Lists UK police fraud types including 419 emails, auction/shopping fraud, courier fraud, cryptocurrency investment fraud, holiday, inheritance, lottery, loan scams, mandate/payment diversion fraud (BEC), recovery fraud, rental, recruitment, romance fraud (also called 'pig butchering'), sextortion, smishing, ticket fraud, vishing and work-from-home scams.

sources.title: Over 70s targeted as courier fraud exceeds £21 million in 2025, with London and Home Counties hit hardest
sources.publisher: Report Fraud / City of London Police
sources.notes: Courier fraud reports rose from 1,721 (2024) to 1,891 (2025); losses from £19.5 million to more than £21 million; average £15,311.08 per victim. People aged 76-96 account for about 62% of reports; London and surrounding regions about 65% of victims. Growing 2025 trend of victims buying gold/jewellery at multiple jewellers over time for a courier, with contact kept up via WhatsApp for days or weeks.

sources.title: Courier fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.publisher: Report Fraud (City of London Police; formerly Action Fraud)
sources.notes: Fake police/bank callers claim a fraudulent card payment, expiring card, corrupt bank staff or a crooked jeweller/currency exchange, then ask victims to withdraw cash, buy expensive items or hand over card and PIN to a courier; they keep the landline open when victims 'call back'. Victims may be told not to discuss it with anyone and to lie to their bank or bypass its security measures. Read via browser (WebFetch 403).

sources.title: Cryptocurrency investment fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Calls crypto investment fraud one of the fastest-growing UK fraud types: social media ads often featuring celebrities, or search ads, lead to professional-looking sites that manipulate prices and returns; victims usually discover the fraud when trying to sell. Red flags are unexpected contact, pressure to invest quickly and unrealistic returns; check firms on the FCA Financial Services Register. Read via browser.

sources.title: Holiday fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Fake adverts, sales calls and messages offer very cheap holidays or short-term lets using stolen property photos, and tell people to pay in cash or by bank transfer or money transfer services that are hard to trace; victims discover at the airport or hotel that nothing was booked. Red flag: being asked to pay by bank transfer or cash; advice is to pay by credit card and check ABTA/ATOL membership. Read via browser.

sources.title: Inheritance fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: A fake overseas lawyer says someone with your surname died leaving a fortune and offers to split it; the fraudsters stress secrecy and speed, then demand successive taxes, legal and banking fees, inventing reasons each time why fees cannot come out of the inheritance and pressuring reluctant victims with how much they have already paid. Read via browser.

sources.title: Loan scams (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Loan scams are advance fee fraud: a fast-loan advert approves anyone regardless of credit history, then demands an upfront fee (e.g. 'insurance' for the loan) and disappears. Advice: check the FCA register and avoid bank transfer payments. Read via browser.

sources.title: Romance fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Romance fraud (also called 'pig butchering') uses fake personas; fraudsters require urgency or secrecy and isolate victims from family and friends, and for almost a third of victims the fraud spans more than a year. Advises never sending money (including vouchers, crypto or 'investments') to an online-only partner and being wary of anyone who asks you not to tell others about them; warns of follow-up recovery fraud. Read via browser.

sources.title: Sextortion (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Financially motivated sexual extortion: an unknown or hacked account quickly moves to explicit chat on an encrypted app, obtains (or fakes with AI) intimate images, then blackmails the victim for money or gift cards. Advises stopping contact, not paying more (payment invites further demands), keeping evidence and reporting to police (101/999) and the platform. Read via browser.

sources.title: Smishing (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
sources.notes: Fake texts (SMS, WhatsApp) lure victims to sites that steal data and money; senders can spoof numbers so messages sit in a genuine bank's thread. Red flags include a delivery company demanding a fee before delivering a parcel, urgent security alerts, and family appeals for money; forward to 7726. Read via browser.

sources.title: Santander's Head Of Fraud targeted as impersonation scams rise by 11%
sources.notes: Describes spoofed calls/texts using a real employee's name (victims told to look the person up on LinkedIn), a claim the account is compromised, and instructions to move money to a 'safe account' and to lie about the payment purpose so the bank cannot give a relevant warning. Santander impersonation losses £10.2 million in Jan-Mar 2023 (+11%), average loss £6,906.

sources.title: Fake Friend Call Scams
sources.notes: Scammers call or WhatsApp from an unknown number, ask the victim to 'guess who' they are, claim a lost phone and new number, then ask for urgent 'loans' for renovation contractors, new-business costs or suppliers, paid via PayNow to unknown persons' accounts; some ask victims to click links or install apps. Advice: verify by calling the friend's last known number. Read via browser.

sources.title: Government Officials Impersonation Scams
sources.notes: Unsolicited calls or WhatsApp video calls from fake SPF or MAS officers accuse victims of crimes and instruct them to transfer money to a 'safe account' for 'investigations', or hand over cash, gold or luxury watches at meet-ups, or show IDs and bank cards on video. Government officials will never ask you to transfer money, disclose bank log-ins, install unofficial apps or transfer your call to the Police; overseas police have no powers to require Singapore residents to assist without government approval. Read via browser.

sources.title: Internet Love Scams
sources.notes: Scammers build weeks or months of online relationship via fake profiles, avoid video calls and meetings, then cite emergencies (business/financial trouble, immigration, rent, oil rigs, machinery, workers' salaries) or fake investments and repeatedly ask for money. Advice: never transfer money or send gift cards to someone you have not met in person.

sources.title: Loan Scams
sources.notes: Fast cash loan ads on TikTok/Facebook or unsolicited SMS/WhatsApp offers lead victims to pay upfront by iBanking transfer, ATM cash deposit, PayNow or cash handover, and the loan is never disbursed. Licensed moneylenders may not advertise this way and must approve loans in person; never pay upfront fees for a loan. Read via browser.

sources.title: Understanding scam types
sources.publisher: ScamShield (Singapore National Crime Prevention Council / SPF)
sources.notes: Read in a browser (old /scams/ URL 404s for WebFetch). Lists 12 scam types: government officials impersonation, investment, job, e-commerce, phishing, fake friend call, loan, tech support, insurance service, internet love, sexual service and cryptocurrency-related scams; states crypto-related scams caused S$182.2M losses in 2025 (20% of reported losses). Tech support entry warns never to grant remote access or approve bank transactions for unsolicited callers.

sources.title: Tech Support Scams
sources.notes: Pop-ups with local-looking numbers lead to fake Microsoft/Apple support who get victims to install AnyDesk, UltraViewer or ConnectWise, log into banking and approve transactions with digital tokens so money can be moved out. Microsoft and Apple never send pop-ups asking you to call; never install remote access apps for unsolicited callers.

sources.title: Business email compromise scams
sources.notes: Scammers pretend to be a business you use and send an invoice with new payee details so a legitimate payment is redirected; warning signs are unexpected bills, supplier payment details changing without notice and slightly altered email addresses. Advice: call the business on an independently sourced number before paying changed details. Read via browser.

sources.title: ACCC warning of suspicious messages as "Hi Mum" scams spike
sources.notes: More than 1,150 Australians lost $2.6 million to 'Hi Mum' scams in the first seven months of 2022, mostly via WhatsApp: the scammer claims a lost or broken phone and new number, builds rapport, then asks for money for an urgent bill, contractor or new phone because they cannot access online banking. 82% of reports came from people over 55, accounting for 95% of losses; advice is to call the number already stored in your phone.

sources.title: Jobs and employment scams
sources.notes: Fake recruiters (posing as big brands, online shopping platforms or agencies) contact people via text, WhatsApp, Signal or Telegram offering easy work-from-home income with no interview, then require them to top up an account with their own money or crypto (USDT) to complete tasks, pay recruitment/training fees, or move money and packages for others (money mules). Advice: never pay to get a job. Read via browser.

sources.title: Money recovery scams
sources.notes: Scammers contact previous victims posing as government agencies, lawyers, police or charities, or run recovery websites and ads, offering to recover stolen money (including tracing crypto) for a fee, percentage or 'tax', then ask for more money for the 'investigation', personal details and remote access. Advice: never accept offers to get your money back; work with your bank. Read via browser.

sources.title: Types of scams
sources.notes: WebFetch returned 403; read in a browser. Lists contact channels (text/SMS, phone, email, social media, website, in-person) and 13 scam types: gambling and betting, phishing, relationship, investment, account or identity takeover, buying and selling, threat, jobs and employment, unexpected money, business email compromise, money recovery, donation scams. Notes text scams can impersonate government, businesses or family and friends.

sources.title: Unexpected money scams
sources.notes: Covers inheritance, rebate, scratchie, travel prize, money transfer and lottery/prize scams in which victims are told they are owed money and must pay an upfront fee, tax or 'administration fee' or share financial/identity details. Government departments and trusted companies never ask for upfront payment to claim a grant or rebate. Read via browser.

sources.title: Scams and Cybercrime Fell by Almost a Quarter in 2025
sources.notes: Summarises the Annual Scams and Cybercrime Brief 2025: scam and cybercrime cases down 24.8% to 41,974; losses S$913.1 million (from S$1.1 billion in 2024); top five by losses were investment, government official impersonation, job, phishing and BEC scams; 81.8% of scams involved self-effected transfers; fake friend call cases and losses fell significantly.

sources.title: Mid-Year Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2026
sources.notes: 1H 2026: 16,821 scam cases (-14.4%), about S$410.6 million lost (-17.9%); 80.8% of scams involved self-effected transfers. Top 10 table gives cases/losses for e-commerce, phishing, investment, job, government officials impersonation (GOIS: 1,363 cases, S$90.8M), social media impersonation, sexual services, loan, internet love and fake friend call scams (353 cases, S$818K). Describes GOIS as bank/telco caller hand-off to fake MAS/MinLaw/SPF officers demanding transfers to 'safety accounts' or cash/gold handovers, plus BEC gift-card variant and courier-redelivery phishing.

sources.title: Keep yourself safe from safe account scams
sources.notes: Safe account scammers impersonate banks, police, the National Crime Agency or an internet provider, may start with smishing/phishing, and may claim the real bank is under investigation and tell victims to lie if their bank calls; some ask for remote access software or cite an overpayment or loan. States no bank, law enforcement or internet provider will ask you to move money to keep it safe; call 159.

sources.title: Annual Fraud Report 2026 (covering 2025 data)
sources.notes: Defines eight APP scam types (malicious payee: purchase, investment, romance, advance fee; malicious redirection: invoice and mandate, CEO, impersonation police/bank staff, impersonation other) with 2025 values: total APP £576.4m (+19%) across 248,070 cases; total fraud £1.28bn. Describes safe-account and 'undercover operation' police/bank impersonation, purchase scams moved off-platform to bank transfer, romance averaging 9.7 payments per scam, and courier scams where cards are handed over on the doorstep.

sources.title: Advisory TAU/ADV/003: Digital arrest
sources.publisher: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), MHA
sources.notes: 'There is no concept of Digital Arrest under any Indian Laws.' Stages: spoofed call, intimidation, digital confinement, money demand

sources.title: Fake SMSs about unpaid electricity bills
sources.notes: Disconnection-tonight SMS from personal numbers; remote-access app requests

sources.title: Cybercriminals using fake customer care numbers
sources.notes: Fake helpline numbers in search results and maps; requests to 'temporarily transfer' funds

sources.title: Cybercrime information 132: KBC lottery fraud
sources.notes: Fake KBC lottery wins on WhatsApp followed by fee demands

sources.title: Message from SBI to update your PAN card details is a scam, do not fall for it
sources.notes: PIB Fact Check called fake an SMS in SBI's name saying the YONO account was closed and asking the customer to update PAN via a link to avoid blocking. SBI never asks for personal details by message; report to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or 1930.

sources.title: Attention Pensioners (home-page notice on cyber fraud calls about Life Certificate)
sources.publisher: Central Pension Accounting Office, Ministry of Finance
sources.notes: CPAO home page warns that cyber fraudsters are calling pensioners about updating their Life Certificate online and asking for personal details and OTPs; CPAO states it does not call for Life Certificate submission or ask for personal information.

sources.title: Duped of Rs 5 lakhs, retired air force personnel becomes victim of 'digital arrest' in Faridabad
sources.notes: Standfirst read (body gated): scammers demanded the victim's bank details and kept him under 'digital arrest', warning him not to disconnect the video call or they would act against his family. Search snippet of the same report: it began with a fake TRAI caller saying his number would be deactivated in two hours over a SIM obtained with his Aadhaar, followed by a fake CBI officer.

sources.title: FedEx courier scam: A tale of terror, trickery, and deceit
sources.notes: Only the standfirst was readable (body gated): data accessed by DH showed 111 FedEx courier scam cases registered up to November 2023, a scam that came to the fore that year (jurisdiction of the count not visible in the standfirst; DH is Bengaluru-based).

sources.title: Centre issues Advisory Against Mobile Calls Impersonating DoT
sources.publisher: ETV Bharat (reporting Department of Telecommunications advisory)
sources.notes: DoT warned of callers in its name threatening that all the citizen's mobile numbers will be disconnected or are being misused in illegal activities, and of WhatsApp calls from foreign numbers (e.g. +92) impersonating officials. DoT authorises no one to make such calls; report on Chakshu (Sanchar Saathi), check connections via 'Know Your Mobile Connections', and call 1930 if defrauded.

sources.title: CBI, ED, Police Don't Arrest People Through Video Calls: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre
sources.notes: Reports an I4C public advisory (5 Oct 2024): CBI, police, customs, ED and judges do not arrest people on video calls. Fraudsters claim the target or a family member is caught in drugs or money laundering, confine them with cameras on, and demand online 'bail' money; report to 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

sources.title: Fact Check: Maharashtra DGIPR Warns Of Fake Electricity Bill Messages, Urges Citizens To Stay Alert
sources.notes: Maharashtra DGIPR and MSEDCL warn of messages threatening power cuts over pending bills and asking consumers to call a personal mobile number. MSEDCL never contacts consumers from personal numbers, uses authorised sender IDs such as VM-MSEDCL, and never asks consumers to download third-party apps; helplines 1912 / 1800-212-3435 / 1800-233-3435.

sources.title: PIB flags fake SBI YONO message urging Aadhaar update, warns customers against phishing scam
sources.notes: PIB Fact Check flagged messages claiming SBI YONO accounts would be blocked over incomplete Aadhaar details unless users installed a KYC-named APK. SBI confirmed it does not ask customers to download APK files for Aadhaar updates; PIB advised not to install apps or APKs sent via email, SMS or WhatsApp.

sources.title: Caution Against Fraudulent/Unauthorised Website Impersonating IRDAI Bima Bharosa/IGMS (Public Notice IRDAI/PPGR/BB/2026-27/25)
sources.publisher: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
sources.notes: IRDAI says igmsirdai.online and irdaiigms.com are not official; the public should not submit personal, policy, banking, KYC or OTP details, or make any payment through such sites, should register insurance complaints only at bimabharosa.irdai.gov.in, and should be cautious of websites, emails, messages or phone calls misusing IRDAI's name or logo.

sources.title: A validated bank account is necessary for credit of refunds (e-Filing portal home-page banner)
sources.publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (incometax.gov.in)
sources.notes: Official banner: refunds are credited only to a validated bank account, which the taxpayer validates by logging in to incometax.gov.in > My Profile > My Bank Account and e-verifying.

sources.title: SCAM ALERT! Don't Fall for Fake Income Tax Emails (e-Filing portal home-page banner)
sources.publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India (incometax.gov.in)
sources.notes: Banner on the official e-Filing home page states that official Income Tax Department communications never contain hyperlinks; any such email should be treated as fraudulent and not clicked, and all services should be accessed via incometax.gov.in.

sources.title: India reports 31 lakh complaints against spam calls and digital arrest scams in 2025; 33,000 numbers blocked
sources.notes: Citing TRAI data: spam-call complaints were 13.62 lakh (2023), 19.38 lakh (2024) and 31.09 lakh (2025), and telcos blocked about 33,000 numbers. Advises victims to tell their bank and mobile provider immediately and report on 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in / Chakshu.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Beware of these 5 SMS, calls
sources.notes: Covers a fake HDFC Bank PAN-update SMS with a short link, WhatsApp free-gift links, and an electricity-bill SMS where UP's chief forest conservator was asked to call a number, install AnyDesk and transfer Re 1, then lost about Rs 1.23 lakh (per IANS). Notes nobody offers bumper returns, bonuses or insurance payouts over the phone.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Beware of electricity bill scam; Rs14.64 lakh withdrawn using Aadhaar fingerprints
sources.notes: Cyberabad police busted a seven-member gang that downloaded property registration documents from the Andhra Pradesh IGRS website, made polymer fingerprints and used an AePS business-correspondent licence to withdraw Rs 14.64 lakh from 149 customers; police said over 10,000 fake fingerprints were prepared and 2,500 cloned prints were seized.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Beware of Aadhaar-enabled Payment System frauds and fake apps
sources.notes: Notes the national cybercrime portal warned of AePS fraud that needs no OTP and advises locking biometrics on the UIDAI website/Aadhaar app; describes a senior citizen whose money was withdrawn via a banking correspondent from an account she never used, Delhi Police findings of silicone fingerprints used to access UIDAI systems, and Telangana police advice to disable Aadhaar biometric linking after AePS fraud.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: From e-Challan, Gas Bill Updates to APK Traps - How Malware Scams Are Draining Bank Accounts
sources.notes: Describes APK campaigns (e.g. 'MParivahan.apk' with a hidden second app overlaying fake banking screens; CERT-In alerted on it) and fake LPG messages saying a booking needs renewal or KYC update to keep cylinder deliveries during a shortage, leading to fake booking/payment pages and 'Gas Bill Update.apk'. Also lists fake income-tax refund alerts leading to phishing sites that capture net-banking passwords; advises using only official OMC apps/portals.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Money extortion scam in the name of customs; beware of fake notices from I4C
sources.notes: Fraudsters posing as Indian Customs (or as social-media/matrimonial contacts 'detained' with a costly gift) demand customs duty into personal bank accounts; PIB says Customs never calls or SMSes asking for duty in personal accounts and genuine communications carry a DIN verifiable on the CBIC site. Also fake emails in the name of the I4C CEO alleging a court order for visiting illegal sites with 24-48 hour deadlines; PIB Fact Check and Cyberdost called them fake.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Payment link scam; be careful of SMS forwarding apps
sources.notes: Reports CloudSEK findings of phishing sites posing as bank complaint portals: a caller posing as a bank executive sends the link and asks for card number, CVV and expiry to issue a 'refund' for a 'failed transaction', then gets an SMS-forwarding app installed to capture OTPs. A traveller who complained about a booking on social media got a fake HDFC call pushing a survey link and an SMS-forwarding app. Advises never searching online for customer-care numbers.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Fake credit card offers, malicious files and new guaranteed income scams
sources.notes: A Facebook 'bank' ad for a lounge-access credit card led to a caller posing as a bank representative who sent a WhatsApp 'form' that was an APK; it captured messages and OTPs and two unauthorised transactions of nearly Rs 50,000 each hit the victim's other cards. Notes genuine bank calls come from 1600-series numbers and bank emails from .bank.in.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Beware, fake emails on tax, criminal action are increasing
sources.notes: Describes a fake email (signed as GST department) telling a taxpayer her tax payment was frozen and asking her to pay a challan via a link, tax phishing peaking around filing/refund season (Income Tax India warned on X on 21 Jul 2024), and a recurring fake 'Office of the Commissioner of Police' email accusing a student of an offence involving minors, with a PDF bearing CBI/IB/cyber-cell logos and fake stamps demanding a reply.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Fake banking apps, cheater e-commerce websites
sources.notes: Delhi Police arrested 23 people in a pan-India network that sent bulk SMS links to fake SBI YONO pages (and in one case a fake KYC-update app), captured credentials, took over accounts and moved money to mule accounts; police found more than 100 such cases, with modules spanning Jamtara, Surat, Kolkata and Delhi NCR.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Govt Schemes Scam
sources.notes: Lists PIB Fact Check-flagged scheme hoaxes: free 'Students' Laptop Scheme 2025' phishing, free recharge, free solar flour mill for rural women requiring Aadhaar and a small registration fee, forged government loan approval letters of Rs 3 lakh demanding a Rs 36,500 'legal insurance charge' (Finance Ministry denied), and fake HPCL/OMC LPG dealership letters (applications only via lpgvitarakchayan.in). Advises never paying registration/processing fees and verifying on .gov.in sites.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Insurance maturity bonus; pay-by-QR code scam
sources.notes: Delhi Police arrested a 32-year-old who, posing as an RBI deputy general manager, told an 82-year-old retired professor his insurance policies had matured with a Rs 90 lakh bonus, demanded a Rs 1.5 lakh processing fee and kept asking for more until the victim had paid Rs 90 lakh (from 2018). Advises verifying directly with the insurer.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: That 'IMP' message from the Income-Tax Department could be a trap
sources.notes: Catalogues fake I-T emails: 'Important Message' notices with fake ITBA reference numbers linking off-portal, fake penalty/prosecution notices with 72-hour deadlines, fake demand notices (PIB flagged an AY25-26 demand and a Rs 6,000 demand as phishing), a Rs 60,000 refund 'manual verification' email PIB flagged as credential theft, and fake e-PAN downloads; CloudSEK reported WhatsApp/email penalty notices delivering OTP-stealing malware. The department never asks for PINs, passwords or OTPs by email/SMS.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Twitter verification mail; beware of calls for updating life certificate
sources.notes: Fraudsters posing as the pension department call pensioners during the November life-certificate season, quoting PPO number, retirement date, Aadhaar and nominee details, and ask for an OTP 'to update the life certificate', then empty the account. CPAO warned pensioners not to respond; life certificates can be given at the bank or via the Aadhaar-based Jeevan Pramaan portal.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: SBI interest certificates and Mahanagar Gas disconnection
sources.notes: WhatsApp messages with Mahanagar Gas logo say supply will be cut tonight at 9:30 pm unless the bill is updated; callers seek a Rs 10 'system update' fee or Rs 1,150 payment, then push 'BILL_UPDATE.apk' and capture banking credentials (one Mumbai man lost about Rs 11.82 lakh). More than 130 MGL customers reportedly targeted since late March with about Rs 3 crore lost; MGL says it never asks for OTPs, bank details or passwords. Also covers fake SBI WhatsApp 'interest certificate' messages.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Beware of bogus websites offering govt schemes, loan on phone
sources.notes: MNRE warned of fake PM-KUSUM (farmer solar pump) portals that rank high in search results; callers quoted Rs 51,000 for a pump and took a Rs 5,600 'registration' payment with a promised refund. Also a Thane loan-on-phone case where fake bank officials demanded processing charges (Rs 7.34 lakh recovered). Verify schemes via official ministry portals or india.gov.in.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: Why Seniors Are in the Crosshairs
sources.notes: Documents senior-citizen losses (e.g. an 82-year-old Delhi man lost Rs 22.92 crore to digital arrest; a 77-year-old Mumbai man paid over Rs 2.25 crore after a fake terror-funding accusation). Victims are told to stay under 'digital custody', not speak to family and not leave home; some refuse to listen to bank staff who flag transfers. Reports that in Nagpur 60% of 2025 cyber-fraud victims were seniors (Rs 45.77 crore lost); suggests a family rule of one call before any large transfer.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: True stories about how people are being cheated everyday
sources.notes: Includes an Andheri businessman who lost Rs 21.17 lakh after responding to a 'Rs 1 international credit card' offer, sharing personal details and approving a Rs 1 transfer through a link; also a fake lottery letter (Rs 11.5 lakh lost over 14 transfers) and Tripura electricity-disconnection SMS warnings.

sources.title: Vietnamese hackers fuelling WhatsApp e-challan scam in India: Report
sources.notes: Reports CloudSEK research: WhatsApp messages impersonating Parivahan Sewa or Karnataka Police deliver a Wromba-family APK that seizes SMS (OTP interception), harvests contacts to spread, and is used to buy and redeem gift cards. Over 4,400 devices infected; one operator's fraud exceeded Rs 16 lakh (271 gift cards, Rs 16,31,000); Gujarat and Karnataka most affected.

sources.title: Govt debunks SMS from India Post asking people to update their address
sources.notes: PIB Fact Check labelled as fake an SMS claiming to be from India Post asking recipients to update their address; India Post does not send such messages for delivery, and people should not click the links.

sources.title: National Scholarship Portal home page announcements
sources.notes: Official NSP announcements: applications for 2026-27 are made on the portal (open from 1 June 2026, student deadline 31 Oct 2026 for listed schemes); NSP services are also available at Common Service Centres, where the total charge for the entire activity per candidate (reference number, biometric authentication, OTR and full application) is fixed at Rs 30 inclusive of taxes. No fraud warning was found on the page.

sources.title: Digital arrests and cyber crimes under watch: over 7.81 lakh SIM cards blocked by Feb
sources.notes: Reports MoS Home Bandi Sanjay Kumar's written reply: digital arrest cases were 39,925 (Rs 91.14 crore) in 2022, 60,676 (Rs 339.03 crore) in 2023, 1,23,672 (Rs 1935.51 crore) in 2024 and 17,718 (Rs 210.21 crore) in 2025 up to 28 Feb.

sources.title: Fake e-challan SMS scam: Kerala Police caution against malicious APKs
sources.notes: Kerala Police warn of SMS from private numbers with realistic e-challan details and a link to a cloned MVD e-challan portal that asks for the vehicle number, shows a fake security check and downloads a malicious APK. Genuine e-challan services never require APK downloads; check only on official MVD/Parivahan portals and report to 1930.

sources.title: SBI Hyderabad saves senior citizen from Rs 13 lakh scam
sources.notes: A 61-year-old doctor under 'digital arrest' came to an SBI branch to break FDs, telling staff it was to buy property; his vague answers raised suspicion. Fraudsters kept him on the phone during branch visits; staff delayed the transaction, asked him to bring a family member, and connected him to 1930.

sources.title: EPFO Urges Members to Avoid Approaching Unauthorized Agents and Use Official EPFO Portals for Free & Secure Online Services
sources.publisher: Ministry of Labour & Employment via PIB (copy hosted on EPFO CDN)
sources.notes: EPFO says cyber-cafe operators and fintech firms are charging members large sums for services that are free, which also exposes members' financial data; all EPFO services (claims, transfers, KYC, grievances) are entirely free and members should not pay third-party agents. Auto-settlement of advance claims was raised to Rs 1 lakh (2.34 crore auto claims in FY 2024-25). PIB Release ID 2136592.

sources.title: Ministry of Labour & Employment Cautions Citizens Against Fake PMVBRY Portals
sources.publisher: Ministry of Labour & Employment via PIB (copy hosted on EPFO CDN)
sources.notes: Ministry disowns websites such as viksitbharatrozgaryojana.org and pmviksitbharatrozgaryojana.com that falsely claim to recruit under the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana; citizens should not share personal information or make payments on such portals; genuine portal is pmvbry.epfindia.gov.in / pmvbry.labour.gov.in. PIB Release ID 2163332.

sources.title: Steps taken to address the issue of digital arrest scams (Rajya Sabha written reply)
sources.publisher: Ministry of Home Affairs via Press Information Bureau
sources.notes: MoS Home Bandi Sanjay Kumar told Rajya Sabha that NCRB does not keep separate digital-arrest data; I4C had blocked more than 3,962 Skype IDs and 83,668 WhatsApp accounts used for digital arrest, and over 7.81 lakh SIMs and 2,08,469 IMEIs were blocked till 28.02.2025. The Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting system had saved over Rs 4,386 crore in 13.36 lakh+ complaints; awareness includes the PM's Mann Ki Baat of 27.10.2024 and 1930 caller tunes. (Opened via HTTP fetch; WebFetch returned 403.)

sources.title: Your Number Will Be Blocked in 2 Hours, Press 9: New Scam Alert! TRAI Issues Warning
sources.notes: Describes an IVR call saying the number will be blocked within two hours and to press 9; a fake TRAI official then says another SIM in the victim's name sent harassing messages, cites a fake FIR, and pushes a police 'clarification', sometimes transferring to fake police. TRAI says it does not call to block numbers.

sources.title: BE(A)WARE - A booklet on Modus Operandi of Financial Fraudsters
sources.publisher: Reserve Bank of India (Office of RBI Ombudsman)
sources.notes: RBI booklet compiled from Ombudsman complaints. Vishing: impostors pose as bankers, insurance agents or government officials, quote a few personal details, and cite urgency (block an unauthorised transaction, stop a penalty) to get OTP/PIN/CVV. Search-engine fraud: fake customer-care numbers for banks, insurers or Aadhaar centres are planted in search results; customer care numbers are never mobile numbers. Also covers SIM swap via fake 3G-to-4G upgrade offers. (rbidocs mirror blocked by bot check; read the rbi.org.in commonman copy.)

sources.title: RBI cautions Public Once Again against Fictitious Offers
sources.notes: RBI states it never contacts the public by unsolicited calls or emails asking for money or personal information, does not hold accounts for individuals or give money to individuals, and warns of people impersonating RBI officials who demand processing fees, tax clearance or conversion charges into specified accounts, followed by escalating demands. (Opened via HTTP fetch.)

sources.title: Raju and the Forty Thieves - pictorial booklet on fraud modus operandi
sources.publisher: Reserve Bank of India (Office of RBI Ombudsman Mumbai-II and CEPD); copy hosted by a bank at scc.bank.in
sources.notes: RBI pictorial booklet of forty fraud stories reported to RBI Ombudsmen/CEPD; only the foreword, index and a few captions are machine-readable. Story titles include KYC phishing link followed by a call and a Rs 50,000 debit, credit card annual fee waiver fake offer, credit card activation fraud, credit card limit upgradation fraud, social welfare scheme fraud, safeguarding your Aadhaar card, and fraud by compromising credentials through search engines.

sources.title: Security - Protect your Card (Types of Frauds)
sources.notes: Issuer's fraud page describes malicious APK files shared via SMS/email/WhatsApp, impersonation of government agencies to get card details, account takeover through shared OTPs (followed by mobile/email change and cross-sell bookings), and screen-sharing fraud where callers posing as the bank have users type card details; states SBI Card will never ask customers to install any third-party application.

sources.title: TRAI issues advisory on frauds misusing TRAI's identity
sources.publisher: SCC Online Blog (reporting TRAI advisory of 6 Aug 2025)
sources.notes: TRAI says it does not investigate consumers, ask for Aadhaar/bank details/OTP, threaten arrest, or initiate contact about number disconnection, and authorises no third party to do so. Fraudsters impersonating TRAI use forged documents, KYC-disconnection threats, digital-arrest tactics, demands for bail/fines/'verification', and fake high-rent mobile tower offers with upfront fees and forged TRAI letters.

sources.title: Telangana vigilance secretary cautions public against digital arrest
sources.notes: Telangana Vigilance secretary Shikha Goel says fake police callers tell victims to isolate themselves and not inform anyone, then ask them to move money to (mule) accounts for 'verification' with a promise it will be returned. She states digital arrest is not a legal process.

sources.title: Telangana electricity board warns people against online fraud
sources.date: on or before 5 Aug 2023 (last modified date)
sources.notes: TSSPDCL cautions about texts saying power will be cut at 9:30 pm because last month's bill was not updated, asking consumers to call an 'electricity officer' who gets them to install Quick Support/AnyDesk and then takes banking and card details. TSSPDCL does not send payment links; pay only via its app or website; call 1930.

sources.title: FedEx scam: Bengaluru software engineer loses Rs 1 crore to fraudsters
sources.notes: A fake FedEx executive said a Taiwan-bound parcel in her name held narcotics and passports at Mumbai airport; fake customs and Mumbai Police took over on Skype, told her to stay in an isolated room with camera on, and had her pay about Rs 1 crore to an 'RBI' account for verification, promising refund within 30 days. FedEx says it does not seek personal information over calls; police note law enforcement does not use Skype.

sources.title: Public Notice: Beware of fraud in the name of TRAI (mobile tower leasing) F. No. 812-4/2012-TD
sources.notes: TRAI notice (linked from its consumer-protection page) says companies/agencies/individuals ask the public to deposit money as 'Government Tax under Telecom Act' for leasing premises for mobile towers, issue fake NOCs purportedly from the Ministry of Communications and IT, and become unreachable after collecting money; TRAI is not involved in any tax/fee on tower leasing or in issuing such NOCs. (Image-only PDF read visually.)

sources.title: Sr citizen loses Rs 1.2L in electricity bill scam
sources.notes: A 66-year-old retired officer got a WhatsApp message that power would be cut at 9:30 pm over an unpaid bill; the fake 'electricity officer' asked him to pay Rs 100 and install 'Quick support', after which Rs 49,000 and Rs 50,000 were debited. PSPCL says it never sends SMS/WhatsApp messages about pending bills.

sources.title: Will deal with iron hand: top court on Rs 3,000 cr extortion via digital arrests
sources.notes: Supreme Court bench (Justice Surya Kant) in its suo motu case said about Rs 3,000 crore had been extorted from victims including senior citizens. Triggered by an Ambala couple (73-year-old woman) defrauded of over Rs 1.05 crore using forged court, ED and PMLA orders with stamps and seals, over audio/video calls with fake CBI/ED/judicial officers.

sources.title: SIM swap, eSIM scams: How scammers can steal your phone number
sources.notes: Reports I4C's warning on eSIM/SIM-swap fraud: impersonators of telecom staff or officials send fake activation links or urgent SIM-swap requests; red flags include sudden loss of signal and missing OTPs. Says I4C reported DoT had blocked 3 to 4 lakh SIM cards used for fraud and advises asking the operator to freeze the SIM if signal drops unexpectedly.

sources.title: NPCI to tighten UPI rules: Peer-to-peer collect feature to end in October
sources.notes: Reports an NPCI circular dated 29 July 2025 directing that from 1 October 2025 UPI P2P collect requests shall not be processed; merchant collect requests continue. Earlier P2P collect had been capped at Rs 2,000 per transaction; the feature had been misused to trick users into approving payments.

sources.title: Cyber Byte (English) July 2025
sources.publisher: Communication & IT Directorate, Central Reserve Police Force (MHA)
sources.notes: Reports the Uttarakhand STF arrest of the alleged mastermind of a Rs 750 crore interstate cyber fraud: a chartered accountant who set up 35-40 shell companies for Chinese operatives and extorted money through fraudulent loan apps (Inst Loan, Maxi Loan, KK Cash, RupeeGo, Lendkar and others), harassing people while posing as company representatives.

sources.title: Cyber Byte (English) March 2025
sources.publisher: Communication & IT Directorate, Central Reserve Police Force (MHA)
sources.notes: CRPF newsletter summarising NPCI's call-merging warning (caller says he got your number from a friend, merges a genuine bank OTP call), a government alert on 'pig butchering'/investment scams targeting unemployed youth, students and housewives that can lead to cyber slavery (citing the MHA annual report), and the SpyLend Android loan-app malware enabling extortion of Indian users.

sources.title: Woman loses Rs 32.8 lakh in part-time work scam
sources.notes: Cyberabad Cyber Crime Police case: a WhatsApp offer of Rs 600-1,000 a day for rating restaurants led to a Telegram 'VIP Task Group'; when withdrawals failed the victim was told to pay for 'task repairs', to release a blocked withdrawal, because her 'credit score' was too low, and to open a bigger withdrawal account, totalling Rs 32,82,573 over 47 transactions; small payouts of Rs 53,139 kept her engaged.

sources.title: NPCI warns users of call merging scam targeting OTPs
sources.notes: Reports NPCI's X (Twitter) warning that scammers use call merging to obtain OTPs: a caller posing as an event organiser or job interviewer claims a mutual friend shared the number and asks the victim to merge a call that is actually the bank's OTP verification call. NPCI advises not merging calls with unknown numbers, notes banks never ask for OTPs on calls, and says to report to 1930.

sources.title: Cyber Crimes - OLX fraud
sources.notes: Describes fraudsters posing as Army/paramilitary personnel buying items on OLX/Quikr, sending a fake payment screenshot, then a QR code and guiding the seller to enter the UPI PIN; each scan debits the seller and the fraudster sends a QR for double the amount to 'fix' it. Advises not to scan a QR code to receive money and to treat urgency and ID cards as warning signs.

sources.title: eSIM scam is targeting users in India: Here's how it happens and how to stay safe
sources.notes: Citing I4C, describes fake eSIM activation calls and links that appear to come from the telecom operator; after the victim clicks, the physical SIM goes dead and calls, SMS and OTPs move to the attacker, who resets passwords and approves UPI payments. Mentions an I4C-reported victim who lost Rs 4 lakh.

sources.title: Cyber gangs exploit job market, Telangana police warn citizens
sources.notes: Hyderabad Cyber Crime Police (DCP Crime) say 26,809 fake job scam cases were registered in Telangana from January 2024 to August 2025. Scammers harvest data from job portals, hold fake interviews, collect registration, insurance and security deposit fees and send fake offer letters; overseas variants include a New Zealand visa-and-job offer. Police say genuine companies do not ask for money before giving a job.

sources.title: Rs 70,000 gone in 15 minutes! Indore man falls for fake bank credit SMS scam
sources.notes: A caller who said he knew the victim personally claimed to transfer Rs 25,000, asked him to check his SMS and forward money to another number; fabricated credit SMSes led to seven transfers totalling Rs 70,000. Police registered a case under BNS sections 318(4) and 319(2).

sources.title: MP News: Scammers con elderly man of Rs 9.25 lakh promising high returns
sources.notes: Indore police cases: a 63-year-old lost Rs 9.25 lakh on a share-trading app promising high returns; a fruit vendor lost Rs 1 lakh while applying for a fake Rs 3 lakh 'PayTM' loan; a youth paid Rs 1.5 lakh in fees for a fake overseas manager job. Police advise not handing phones to strangers claiming to be bank staff and verifying overseas jobs before paying fees.

sources.title: 336 fake APKs linked to Rs 125 crore fraud: Gujarat Police nab Jamtara gang members
sources.notes: Surat City Cyber Crime Cell case: fake APKs posing as bank apps (e.g. a fake PNB One), PM-Kisan, RTO challans, customer support and hospitals were spread via WhatsApp and Telegram; police analysed 336 APKs linked to 5,613 compromised devices and 1,06,643 debit transactions worth about Rs 125.39 crore, with money routed to mule accounts.

sources.title: Fraud Alert: UPI Is Fast & Convenient, but One Careless Tap Can Cost You Dearly
sources.notes: Describes current UPI tricks: QR codes sent on WhatsApp promising a refund or cashback, collect requests saying money is waiting to be collected, fake customer care asking to install remote-access apps or approve UPI requests, fake payment screenshots and tampered shop QR codes. Notes RBI's framework links customer liability to prompt reporting (within three working days).

sources.title: UPI Safety Shield
sources.notes: NPCI safety page (JavaScript-rendered; WebFetch returned only the title). Search snippet states UPI PIN is needed only to deduct money and is not required for receiving money, and to scan QR codes only when making a payment.

sources.title: Palghar bank official duped of Rs 46.41 lakh in stock trading fraud
sources.notes: MBVV Police case: victim added to WhatsApp investment groups by people posing as executives of reputed firms, shown a fake SEBI registration certificate and told to install apps via links; the app showed Rs 8.12 crore profit on Rs 46.41 lakh invested, and withdrawal required an extra 10 per cent 'tax'.

sources.title: NPCI cautions consumers against downloading AnyDesk app
sources.notes: Reports RBI Alert 1/2019 (14 Feb 2019) on fraud using remote screen access apps and NPCI's caution: fraudsters get victims to install AnyDesk, share the 9-digit code and grant permissions, then use the victim's payment and banking apps. NPCI's risk head advised never giving anyone access to your handset through such apps.

sources.title: Bengaluru entrepreneur narrowly escapes this SMS scam: how to not fall for this old-school technique
sources.notes: A caller posing as the father's elderly acquaintance said his transfer to the father failed, sent fake credit SMSes (Rs 10,000 then Rs 30,000) from a 10-digit number, claimed he sent Rs 30,000 instead of 3,000 by mistake and asked for Rs 27,000 back urgently, citing a hospital/medical emergency.

sources.title: I4C warns investors against fake WhatsApp stock tips, fake trading apps
sources.notes: Reports I4C's July 2026 advisory: fraudsters add people to WhatsApp/Telegram groups with 'VIP stock tips' and guaranteed returns, send fake trading app links that show fabricated profits, and on withdrawal block the account or demand taxes, processing or verification fees. I4C says genuine brokers never require extra deposits to release funds; cites a retired Mumbai scientist who lost Rs 1.3 crore.

sources.title: Curbing Cyber Frauds in Digital India (PIB backgrounder)
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India
sources.notes: Government backgrounder: notes organised fraud linked to 'fraud factories' in Southeast Asia (citing ED), online betting apps that lured users into wallet deposits generating over Rs 400 crore of criminal proceeds, the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act passed 21 Aug 2025 banning online money gaming, over 9.42 lakh SIM cards and 2,63,348 IMEIs blocked, and CFCFRMS/1930 saving over Rs 5,489 crore across 17.82 lakh complaints.

sources.title: Postal Department issues advisory warning about fake job rackets
sources.notes: PIB page returned HTTP 403. Search snippet: India Post warns that fake selection orders are being issued and states it does not ask, solicit or accept any money from applicants.

sources.title: The Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Bill, 2018 (bill track)
sources.notes: Summarises the BUDS Bill: deposit schemes not registered with a listed regulator are banned; running one carries 2-7 years' imprisonment and Rs 3-10 lakh fine, defaulting 3-10 years and up to twice the amount collected; inducing depositors by falsifying facts is an offence; a Competent Authority can attach property and a Designated Court distributes proceeds; an online database of deposit takers is provided for.

sources.title: Money transferred by mistake? Fake credit SMS scam (WebQoof decode)
sources.notes: Describes a January 2025 attempt: a caller claiming to be the victim's father's friend said the father asked him to send money via Google Pay; a fake SMS showing Rs 30,000 credited arrived from a personal mobile number, and the caller said he sent 30,000 instead of 3,000 by mistake and asked for the difference back. Advises verifying with the named relative and checking the bank sender ID; reporting via Chakshu (Sanchar Saathi) or 1930.

sources.title: BE(A)WARE - A Booklet on Modus Operandi of Financial Frauds (press release)
sources.notes: RBI press release launching the BE(A)WARE booklet, which covers SIM swaps, phishing/vishing links, lottery frauds and fake loan websites/apps. RBI says customers sharing confidential information, knowingly or unknowingly, is a major cause of fraud. The booklet PDF itself (rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/content/pdfs/BEAWARE07032022.pdf) was behind a bot check and could not be opened.

sources.title: Raju and The Forty Thieves (RBI Kehta Hai)
sources.notes: RBI pictorial booklet and videos on fraud modus operandi; page redirected bots to the RBI home page. Search snippet lists entries including QR code scams, illegal loan apps, fraudsters posing as recovery agents, social welfare scheme fraud and online job fraud.

sources.title: Nearly 7,000 Indians rescued from Cambodia, Myanmar, Laos cybercrime compounds since 2022: Centre
sources.notes: Reports MoS External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh's written reply in Parliament: 6,998 Indians rescued from cybercrime compounds in 2022-2025 (Cambodia 2,533; Laos 2,297; Myanmar 2,168), lured by fake job offers from dubious firms via unscrupulous agents and illegal channels. MEA advises using only government-authorised recruiting agents.

sources.title: Advisory Against investment in Fraudulent Trading Schemes claiming to be offered to Indian residents by FPIs (PR No. 53/2025)
sources.publisher: Securities and Exchange Board of India
sources.notes: SEBI press release (copy hosted by HDFC Mutual Fund) warning about social media, WhatsApp, Telegram and apps offering market access via FPIs/FIIs, with claims of an 'institutional trading account', discounted or guaranteed IPO allotment, anchor book access and discounted block trades. SEBI says the FPI route is unavailable to resident Indians (limited exceptions) and to verify registration on sebi.gov.in.

sources.title: Google rolls out on-device scam detection in India as digital fraud losses top Rs 70 billion
sources.notes: Google piloted Android alerts with Navi, Paytm and Google Pay that warn users who open financial apps while screen sharing during a call, with options to end the call or stop sharing. Cites an MHA estimate of Rs 70 billion digital-fraud losses in the first five months of 2025.

sources.title: Hyderabad man duped of Rs 1.95 lakh via fake PM Kisan APK
sources.notes: A Yousufguda resident installed a 'PM Kisan' APK received on WhatsApp from an unknown number in late July 2025; his phone was hacked, messages were sent to his contacts and Rs 1.95 lakh was debited. Hyderabad Cybercrime Police registered a case.

sources.title: Googling customer care numbers? Be warned of scammers, says Hyd police advisory
sources.notes: Reports a Hyderabad police advisory on fake customer care numbers found via Google and Justdial: a Zomato customer seeking a refund shared bank details and UPI PIN and lost Rs 70,000; an airline customer was asked to pay Rs 75 via Google Pay, then for card details. Police say genuine customer care never asks for card, OTP or UPI PIN details.

sources.title: Govt blocks 100 websites involved in job scams, illegal investments
sources.notes: Reports the MHA statement that I4C's National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit identified 100+ overseas-run websites for task-based part-time job and illegal investment frauds, blocked by MeitY. Modus operandi: Google/Meta ads such as 'Ghar baithe job', a WhatsApp/Telegram agent, like/subscribe or map-rating tasks with small commissions, then larger deposits that get frozen. Targets: retired employees, women and unemployed youth; proceeds moved via mule/rented accounts, cards, crypto and overseas ATMs.

sources.title: Gurugram police warns against 5G fraud
sources.notes: Gurugram Police reported the city's first 5G-upgrade fraud on 1 Oct 2022: scammers posing as telecom executives send a link and gain access to phones on the pretext of upgrading to 5G. Police advised never sharing OTPs and reporting to 1930.

sources.title: Gurugram police nab two in WhatsApp trading scam
sources.notes: Gurugram Cyber Police traced Rs 25 lakh from a WhatsApp stock-trading fraud to an account whose holder had sold it for a 2% commission on money passing through; the buyer, a former private bank manager, sold his own account for 4%. Both were arrested; police said 33 bank employees had been arrested in cyber fraud cases.

sources.title: Invited to wedding? Police say check the link before you click
sources.notes: Himachal Pradesh SP (Cybercrime) warns that fake wedding invitations arrive on WhatsApp as APK files or phishing links; the malware steals photos, contacts and banking details and forwards similar invites to the victim's contacts. Police say genuine wedding cards are JPG or PDF files, never APKs; report on 1930.

sources.title: Saradha Group financial scandal
sources.notes: Encyclopaedic summary: a group of 200+ companies in eastern India ran a Ponzi-style collective investment scheme mislabelled as a chit fund, selling high-return deposits through commission agents; it collapsed in April 2013 after collecting an estimated Rs 200-300 billion from about 1.7 million depositors, leading to SEBI Act amendments and a CBI probe.

sources.title: Matrimonial fraud: MHA I4C warns of fake profiles on marriage sites (Hindi)
sources.notes: Reports an I4C (MHA) warning that fraudsters create fake matrimonial profiles posing as NRIs, doctors, engineers, army officers or businessmen, build emotional bonds and propose quickly, then ask for money for customs duty on gifts, travel/visa costs or emergencies. Red flags include avoiding video calls and emotional pressure; advises no money transfers before meeting, reverse image search and reporting to 1930.

sources.title: Disclaimer (fake websites using the Amul name)
sources.notes: Amul warns that fraudsters use its brand, logo and address on fake websites to deceive the public, and advises people not to send money, personal information or bank details to anyone claiming to represent or be associated with Amul; verify via Amul's business office or www.amul.com. It does not specifically describe franchise fees.

sources.title: Defending Against Frontier AI Driven Cyber Risks (CIAD-2026-0020)
sources.notes: High-severity CERT-In advisory on AI-enabled cyber risks. For individuals it warns that AI-generated deepfakes and impersonation can be highly convincing and advises verifying voice calls, video messages and urgent requests, especially where money or sensitive information is involved. It does not detail family-impersonation scripts.

sources.title: Comn. & IT Directorate CRPF cyber newsletter: MHA's I4C issues alert on online booking scams targeting pilgrims, tourists
sources.notes: Summarises an I4C nationwide alert on online booking frauds mostly hitting religious pilgrims and tourists: fake websites, social media pages, WhatsApp accounts and sponsored Google/Facebook ads offering Kedarnath helicopter bookings, Char Dham yatra, guest house/hotel stays, cabs and religious tour packages. Also reports a Hyderabad Shaadi.com fake-profile case (Rs 11 lakh plus blackmail).

sources.title: Cops monitor dubious Ram Mandir links
sources.notes: Hyderabad cybercrime police warned before the Ayodhya consecration about dubious links promising live photos and fraudulent QR codes soliciting donations, cautioning that such links can expose phones and bank accounts.

sources.title: Techie catfished of Rs 81.67 lakh, 2 arrested
sources.notes: Andhra Pradesh police arrested two people after a software employee met a woman on Instagram who claimed to be in love with him, gradually gained his trust and allegedly took Rs 81.67 lakh from him.

sources.title: Cheating scams
sources.notes: Advance-fee lures (lottery wins, money-transfer commissions, overseas jobs, throwaway-price goods, hacked contacts pleading for money) followed by fees, taxes or transport costs. Advises verifying any contact through an independently sourced number and never paying upfront to unknown parties.

sources.title: FaceBook friendship frauds
sources.notes: Fraudsters befriend victims on Facebook or matrimonial sites, move to foreign-code VoIP calls, promise expensive gifts by courier, then a fake Indian Customs caller demands customs charges and GST for cash or jewellery in the parcel, backed by fake receipts and tracking sites; a variant uses a fake ticket and the 'foreigner' detained at the airport. Advises never depositing money on such instructions, even small amounts.

sources.title: FaceBook SOS frauds
sources.notes: Scammers clone or hijack a real Facebook profile and message the person's friends: an SOS for urgent money for a hospital or accident with repayment promised in a day or two, a fake lottery, or a donation appeal for a needy person. Advises calling the person directly and treating any money request over Messenger as immediately suspect.

sources.title: Fake government website frauds
sources.notes: Fraudsters create sites imitating government portals and schemes, advertising jobs, subsidies or benefits and collecting registration, examination or verification fees. Advises verifying with the department or PIB Fact Check and not trusting emblems/logos as proof.

sources.title: Fake shopping site frauds
sources.notes: Fake shopping sites copy known brands or pose as new stores offering very low prices and take online payment but never deliver, or send used items; a variant promises a free gift and then 'customer service' demands refundable handling or GST fees. Advises suspicion of deep discounts, checking reviews and preferring cash on delivery on untested sites.

sources.title: Gift card frauds
sources.notes: Fraudsters impersonate the victim's boss or a senior person by email or text and ask them to buy Amazon gift cards and send the claim codes, citing employee incentives, client appreciation or charity, while claiming to be busy, travelling or unreachable so the request cannot be checked. Advises verifying via a known channel and treating urgency as a tell-tale sign.

sources.title: KBC lottery fraud
sources.notes: WhatsApp messages, mostly from +92 numbers, claim the recipient won Rs 25 lakh in a KBC-Jio lottery and must contact a 'manager', who asks for refundable processing charges and GST into various bank accounts, keeps 'raising' the prize and demands more for weeks. Notes genuine lotteries deduct tax from the prize, warns against callers who insist on secrecy and against skipping a talk with family.

sources.title: Lottery scam
sources.notes: Describes lottery/prize and commission emails, SMS and calls where victims are drawn in gradually and asked to pay transfer fees, taxes or transport costs in stages, money going to offshore or Indian carrier accounts. Advises never responding to fake lottery wins and never sending money to unknown people for promised returns.

sources.title: Sextortion frauds
sources.notes: Criminals using fake profiles on dating apps, matrimonial sites or Instagram build rapport, push for intimate images or sex chats/nude video calls which they record, then demand money (sometimes lakhs) threatening to upload it or send it to family and friends. Advises preserving evidence and filing a police complaint; warns to be wary when someone pushes quickly toward intimacy.

sources.title: Social media crimes
sources.notes: Lists fake/impersonation profiles of known persons, account hacking used to deceive contacts, and 'fake online friendship' scams where fraudsters build an emotional bond and then ask for money citing medical emergencies, legal trouble or problems abroad. Advises refusing strangers' requests and asking platforms to remove fake profiles while warning contacts.

sources.title: Kerala woman duped of Rs 12 lakh in customs scam: Government reveals how this fraud works
sources.notes: Reports a PIB Fact Check warning that Indian Customs never calls or SMSes asking for duty to be paid into personal bank accounts, and a Kerala woman who lost Rs 12 lakh after paying an initial Rs 15,000 'duty' on a gift and then escalating amounts. PIB quote: Indian Customs never call/SMS to pay duty in personal accounts.

sources.title: I4C detects two latest cyber crime trends in India
sources.publisher: ETV Bharat (reporting I4C National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit advisory)
sources.notes: I4C's threat analytics unit flagged fake profiles on matrimonial and dating platforms (Shaadi.com, Jeevansathi, Tinder, Bumble) posing as well-off NRIs or armed-forces personnel, filtering targets by age and income, building trust via calls and WhatsApp video, then creating urgent situations to push money or fake crypto investments. Advises reverse image search and not sending money to people not met in person.

sources.title: Cyber Crime Cell issues advisory against fake calls
sources.publisher: The Goan (Goa Police Cyber Crime Cell advisory)
sources.notes: Goa Police Cyber Crime Cell warned of 'virtual kidnapping' calls, often from foreign or VPN numbers, telling parents their child was kidnapped, in an accident or in police custody and demanding money for release. Advises staying calm, verifying directly with the child, not sending money, and reporting to police and Sanchar Saathi.

sources.title: Avoid unknown video calls: Cyber police warn amid rising sextortion cases
sources.publisher: The Hitavada (Bhopal Cyber Crime Police advisory)
sources.notes: Bhopal Cyber Crime police advisory: criminals build trust through fake social media and dating-app profiles, record obscene video calls, then threaten to send the material to family and friends. Advises rejecting unknown video calls, not paying blackmailers because payment does not end the demands, preserving evidence and reporting to 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

sources.title: Advisories (I4C advisory listing page)
sources.publisher: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), MHA
sources.notes: Index of I4C/NCTAU public advisories including matrimonial-platform crypto fraud (Oct 2025), 'Boss scam' executive impersonation (Jun 2026), hacked WhatsApp accounts (Jan 2022), army-personnel rental fraud (Jul 2022), travel/holiday fraud (Aug 2021), bogus giveaways (Aug 2021), romance frauds via dating apps (Aug 2021) and KBC lottery frauds (Sep 2021).

sources.title: Cybercriminals committing Business Partnership scam to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-125)
sources.notes: A fraudster posing as a wealthy foreign investor offers a business partnership in India and promises lakhs to set it up, but first asks the victim to deposit money in various accounts for documentation, customs and other taxes, then disappears.

sources.title: Cybercriminals defrauding citizens going on holiday as travel restrictions ease (Cyber Crime Information-127)
sources.notes: Fraudsters use fake travel ads on social media, impersonate travel agents or airlines offering big discounts, and build fake travel and holiday-accommodation websites misusing names like MakeMyTrip and Airbnb; victims pay and contact stops. Advises checking URLs for slight domain changes and that deals too good to be true usually are.

sources.title: Bogus giveaway scam (Cyber Crime Information-129)
sources.notes: Bogus giveaways of phones, travel packages or crypto are promoted on YouTube, Instagram and SMS; victims are asked to pay a transfer or administrative fee, sometimes on a forged website that also harvests bank details. Advises never paying fees for giveaways.

sources.title: Romance Frauds perpetrated through dating apps (Cyber Crime Information-130)
sources.notes: Fraudsters create fake dating/social-media profiles, use 'love bombing', move the chat off the app to phone or messaging, and once trusted ask for money, gifts, bank details or intimate pictures/videos; often part of criminal networks. Advises not sending money or documents to unknown people.

sources.title: Cybercriminals using fake restaurant websites to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-131)
sources.notes: Fraudsters clone restaurant or fast-food franchise websites; customers pay but nothing arrives and card/bank details are harvested; sites change URLs when reported. Advises ordering only from known sites, checking spelling/domain age and confirming with the business.

sources.title: Cybercriminals hacking WhatsApp accounts to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-145)
sources.notes: Explains WhatsApp takeover by tricking victims into merging a verification call or sharing the activation OTP, then using the hijacked account to message all contacts and groups with requests like being hospitalised and needing money, plus extortion. Advises two-step verification and that friends and relatives should not respond to money requests from such accounts.

sources.title: Fraudsters using Army personnel details to perpetrate financial cyber frauds (Cyber Crime Information-159)
sources.notes: From NCRP complaints: fraudsters posing as newly posted Army officials target owners advertising on 99acres, Housing.com and social media, claim the deposit can only be paid via the 'Army bank', ask victims to send small verification amounts and then send UPI 'request money' collects that victims approve thinking they will receive money. States that OTP/PIN entry is for sending money, not receiving.

sources.title: Cyber Surakshini: book on cybercrime against women
sources.notes: I4C awareness book (image PDF, read visually). Online sextortion page advises not engaging or paying because it leads to further demands, and reporting at cybercrime.gov.in/1930. Voice cloning page describes a mother tricked by an AI clone of her son's voice asking for emergency money and advises a family code word and not acting on money requests without confirmation. Romance scam page describes a 'professional working abroad' on a dating platform who avoids meetings or video verification and then claims an emergency.

sources.title: Spot the Scam Before the Scam Spots You (brochure)
sources.notes: I4C brochure (image PDF, read visually). Sextortion: scammers record private photos or video calls, starting from chats on social media/dating sites or unknown video calls; advice is do not pay and report. WhatsApp scam: a contact's hijacked handle sends an OTP 'by mistake' and asks you to forward it, which hijacks your account. Dating app scam: fake profiles ask for money or push investment, sometimes leading to blackmail.

sources.title: Misuse of Matrimonial Platforms for Investment/Crypto Frauds (TAU/ADV/006)
sources.publisher: I4C National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, MHA
sources.notes: Based on NCRP complaint analysis, fraudsters create fake profiles with stolen or morphed photos on Jeevansathi, Shaadi, Matrimony.com and dating apps, pose as professionals abroad, in the armed forces or reputed firms, filter targets by age and income, build intimacy via calls and WhatsApp video (often with edited backgrounds), then create urgent or emotional situations to solicit money or crypto 'investments'.
